beats.text: Some things are quicker to {say}say than to click. K-Desktop understands spoken orders, {local}entirely on your PC.
Let's {setup}set it up, {commands}say a few commands, {dictate}dictate some text, and finally, {hands}talk without touching anything.
Open {settings}Settings, Voice, and turn it {on}on. The voice models are {download}downloaded once, just under a gigabyte, and they {free}free their memory when you're not using them.
Pick your {mic}microphone, and give it a {hotkey}hotkey to talk. Keep {echo}Ignore what the PC is playing on, so music or a film won't drown you out.
And {private}neither your audio nor your words ever leave the PC.
Hold the hotkey and say what you want. Now, {finding}finding the command you meant.

First, it reads the {words}words. It looks for a command's {name}name in what you said. It ignores {filler}filler words like please, different word {endings}endings, small {slips}slips, and words that just {sound}sound alike. {youtube}You tube becomes YouTube.

When the words aren't enough, it looks at the {meaning}meaning. {gemma}EmbeddingGemma, a small model from Google, turns sentences into {vectors}vectors: points in a {space}space where similar meanings sit close together.
So, {clean}clean out the trash lands right next to your command, {empty}Empty Recycle Bin. Without a single list of synonyms.

It also knows what isn't yours. {tv}Turn off the TV is close to {shutdown}Shut down the computer, but it's even closer to a list of {everyday}everyday requests that K-Desktop doesn't handle. So {nothing}nothing happens. Anything that {powers}powers off the PC has to be said especially clearly.
And when it isn't sure, it doesn't guess. It {shows}shows what it heard, and the command it {thinks}thinks you meant, and {nothing}does nothing.
You can {chain}chain orders, too. {open}Open YouTube {and}and empty the recycle bin, runs both.
Music and volume work without any command at all. {pause}Pause. {next}Next song. {quieter}A little quieter. {forty}Volume to forty percent. {play}Play music.
{dictation}Dictation types what you say wherever the cursor is. While you talk, say {newline}new line, {scratch}scratch that, or {stopd}stop dictating.
Start it with its {hotkey}own hotkey, or simply say {say}start dictating.
One last tip: there's more than one way to {voice}talk to it, all {local}on your PC, with {internet}no internet.
Push to talk: {hold}hold the voice hotkey while you speak. Or {tap}tap it once, and just talk: it {stops}stops when you go quiet.
Or use a {wake}wake word. {kd}K-Desktop, open the browser. {nokey}No key at all.
And from the couch, use your {phone}phone as the microphone: in the web app, or with the {android}Android app's own microphone.

The wake word is yours, and you record it in {wakewords}Settings, Wake words, in under a minute. {silence}Three seconds of silence, to measure the background noise. {word}The word itself, several times. And {speech}ten seconds of normal speech, so everyday conversation never sets it off. It can even be a {madeup}made-up word.
Next up: {next}calendar and mail.
Thanks for watching.
